subtopic: ENLISTMENT OR RECRUITING OF CANADIANS FOR FOREIGN MILITARY SERVICE-EXPORT OF MUNITIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ENLISTMENT OR RECRUITING OF CANADIANS FOR FOREIGN MILITARY SERVICE-EXPORT OF MUNITIONS
speechtext: I wish to direct a question -to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I am informed that during the regular nightly CBC news broadcast on Wednesday of this week at 10.45 p.m. eastern standard time it was stated that the government of Canada contemplated the passing of an order in council giving effect to the Imperial Foreign Enlistment Act of 1870 in Canada, with a view to the prohibition of Canadian volunteers fighting in Spain. I wish to inquire whether, and if so why, a decision of such importance is to be dealt with by order in council without first ascertaining the will of parliament now in session.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ENLISTMENT OR RECRUITING OF CANADIANS FOR FOREIGN MILITARY SERVICE-EXPORT OF MUNITIONS
speechtext:
The	hon.	gentleman was kind
enough to give notice of this question. No order in council has been passed regarding enlistment in the armed forces in Spain or elsewhere, nor has the government contemplated passing any such order in council without first bringing the question before parliament.
In order to make the information more complete, and as it relates to the same subject, on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) I desire to answer immediately a question asked by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Gariepy), being question No. 19 on the order paper, which reads:
1.	Has the government given consideration
to a speech delivered by the Honourable Maurice Duplessis at Three Rivers and published verbatim in "Le Devoir" of January 26, 1937, in which he said:	.	.
"I declare that in our province communistic recruiting has been going on, that our young men have been enrolled to fight for the communists in Spain, that Canadian passports have been procured for them for Spanish ports, not for one or two young men, but for several, which shoivs that an organization exists, and indicates that there is something lacking somewhere."
2.	Is it the intention of the government to investigate these assertions concerning the issue of passports, as mentioned in this speech.
In reply to a question by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Elliott) on January 19, I stated:
In view of recent developments, the question w'hether any special action should be taken regarding the control of enlistment m Canada for military service in foreign countries has been under examination. Canada is not included in the twenty-seven countries, all European states, which are represented on the non-intervention committee organized to deal with the Spanish situation, and which has made recommendations to the governments represented thereon for the prohibition of the substantial enlistment on both sides m the Spanish conflict which has taken place from European centres. The question, however, will continue to be given consideration.
I added that something more would be said on the subject later on. The whole question of the control of enlistment as well as the related question of the export of munitions has been under consideration by the government for some time past. As regards enlistment, members of the house are aware that the Foreign Enlistment Act, passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom in 1870, extends to Canada. The government concluded it would be desirable to propose Canadian legislation on this subject. After examination of the question by a technical committee, instructions were given for the drafting of a bill, which will shortly be introduced.

Home Improvement Loans
As regards application to Spain, I may say that the main section of the act, section 4, provides a penalty for enlistment or inducement of enlistment of a British subject within or without His Majesty's dominions, in the military or naval service of any foreign state at war with any foreign state at peace with His Majesty; the fifth section provides penalties for embarking for such purpose, and other sections deal with shipbuilding and fitting out naval or military expeditions against the dominions of any friendly state. It had been generally held that the prohibition of enlistment or recruiting did not apply to a civil war. This month, in pursuance of its endeavours to secure the acceptance by European states of the policy of non-intervention in Spain, the government of the United Kingdom issued a statement indicating its opinion that the act, and particularly the sections penalizing enlistment or inducement, or embarking for the purpose of such enlistment, are applicable in the case of the present conflict in Spain. As the Canadian government had already decided to introduce legislation on the general subject, it was considered advisable to deal with such specific questions in that connection.
As regards the issue of passports, I am informed that for some months past no application for a passport has listed Spain among the countries to be visited, and no passport has been issued to any person who has indicated Spain as one of the countries of destination. The procedure as to passports will be brought into conformity with any legislation that may be passed by parliament.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into 31111-25J
committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to guarantee approved lending institutions against losses which they may sustain as a result of home improvement loans made by them, to limit the liability of the government of Canada in respect of such guarantees to not exceeding fifteen per centum of the aggregate amount of home improvement loans made by any such approved lending institution and to not exceeding seven million five hundred thousand dollars.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will give us as clear an explanation as he can of the whole situation. I thought it might be preferable that that be done now, when questions may be asked if necessary, rather than that time should be taken up in a discussion of the matter before going into committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
At this stage would the committee prefer a general statement, which later could be dealt with when the bill is in committee? Details can be much better examined, of course, when the bill has been brought down, but I agree that in connection with new legislation it is desirable at this stage of the proceedings to indicate broadly what is proposed.
The bill which this resolution precedes is designed to secure legislative sanction for the administration of a plan which has become widely known as the home improvement plan. Briefly stated, the bill asks authority to give a limited government guarantee to loans made in accordance with certain stipulated conditions which will be found in detail in the bill itself, by approved lending institutions for the purpose of making repairs, additions and improvements to urban and rural homes. The guarantee is to be limited to fifteen per cent of the total amount of the loans made by any approved lending institution, and in any case the authority to the government to guarantee is limited to $7,500,000 in the aggregate. This means that the total amount of loans to be subject to guarantee can not exceed $50,000,000. In the bill also, Mr. Chairman, will be found a provision reserving to the government the right to announce at any time that no further loans will be guaranteed.
The plan itself is based upon a recommendation made by the National Employment Commission as a result of extensive investigations into methods of absorbing the unemployed in this country, and into the operation of a similar plan in the United States of America during the past two years.
a
Home Improvement Loans

The recommendation was made by the commission and accepted by the government on the 9th of September, 1936, on which occasion the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a public announcement in which he stated that the plan in its financial aspects would require parliamentary sanction under new legislation and that such legislation would be introduced into parliament at this session.
The announcement made by the Prime Minister on that occasion met with an enthusiastic response in, I think, all sections ^ of the country. Many requests were received that the plan should be made effective at once in order that its beneficial effects might accrue during the winter months when unemployment tends to be most severe. Under date of September 28 the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, acting on behalf of all the chartered banks, wrote to me as Minister of Finance stating that the banks had agreed to cooperate fully with the dominion government in carrying out the plan, and moreover that they were willing to commence making loans on their merits without awaiting the legislation, provided they had the assurance that the necessary legislation would be introduced and that it would be in such form as to make the dominion guarantee retroactive to cover loans made in accordance with the approved conditions prior to the passing of the necessary legislation.
The plan as originally announced had suggested a financing' charge not in excess of the discount rate of five per cent for a one-year loan repayable in equal monthly instalments, and proportionate rates of course for longer periods. This was the maximum originally contemplated by the employment commission, and is the rate which was and is still allowed under the United States scheme. While the five per cent rate was intended by the employment commission only to be the maximum, and while such small instalment loans entail a great deal of detail work by way of both investigation and collection, it appeared to the government to be unnecessarily high for the effective working of the plan. Representatives of the banks were therefore called for conference at Ottawa to discuss their offer of immediate assistance and to consider the conditions which would have to be imposed in order to make the loans eligible for guarantee, including the maximum interest charge.
I would be stretching the truth somewhat if I were to say that the banks enthusiastically welcomed the government's proposal to reduce the maximum financing charge from a

five per cent to a three and a quarter per cent discount rate, but I can at least pay the tribute to the banks that when they were fully apprised of the government's intention and desire to make the plan a complete success, they willingly accepted the low interest rate as their contribution to a great national cooperative undertaking, and assured us that they would give the government their wholehearted cooperation in making the plan a real success. I think it is a matter of common knowledge that in the last few months the banks and other lending institutions have been living fully up to this undertaking.
When the conditions imposed had been accepted by the banks, under date of October 15, I wrote to the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association giving him the assurance that the government would introduce the necessary legislation at the next session of parliament, and that the legislation would be introduced in such form as to make the guarantee retroactive to cover loans made prior to the passing of such legislation, provided the loans were made in conformity with conditions approved by the Department of Finance and conditions which, of course, will be embodied in the legislation. On the basis of this assurance the home improvement plan has been in operation since about November 1, and the figures as to loans from November 1 to December 31, during the first two months of operation, as reported to the Department of Finance, indicate that up to that time 81,-
200,000	has been loaned in small amounts, and that, if my memory serves me correctly, about 3,600 loans had been made during that time.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Has the minister the figures as to loans to provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
I have not that information before me, but will have it when we are in committee on the bill. I shall have information by provinces, by cities, the average amount of loans, and analyses of any kind that might reasonably be issued from the standpoint of information required. However I have not the information sought at this stage, and am attempting merely to give a general survey.
I believe the first two months' experience should assure the committee as to the future success of the plan, and I believe there is wisdom in putting it into operation during the late fall and early winter months. I am sure the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) will confirm the opinion of the employment commission. After studying the matter exhaustively they have found that approximately eighty cents out of every dollar ex-

Home Improvement Loans
pended in the project is expended on labour used at some stage of the proceedings. When the bill is under discussion I shall be pleased to table the correspondence with the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association.
Perhaps it is sufficient for me to say at this time that the plan provides for loans to owners of rural and urban homes in order to assist them in financing repairs, additions and improvements. The loans shall not exceed $2,000 on any single property. A provision in the bill to be laid before the house, however, will suggest a somewhat higher maximum with regard to multiple family houses. Another provision will be that the loans shall be made for terms not in excess of three years, except with respect to loans in excess of $1,000, where the maximum term may be five years. All loans are repayable by equal monthly or other convenient periodic instalments.
The bill will provide that the maximum financing charge shall not exceed a discount rate of three and a quarter per cent for a one-year loan repayable in equal monthly instalments, and proportionate rates for longer periods. The loans are based on the character and income of the borrower, and no security by way of collateral or endorsement is required. Furthermore we have attempted to devise a simple procedure in order that the plan may be available to home owners in every community, with a maximum of convenience and economy.
Although I believe the purposes behind the development of the home improvement plan are familiar to all, they may be described as (1) to absorb unemployment, particularly in the building trades where unemployment is most heavily concentrated; (2) to stimulate a revival of the construction industry, which, as every hon. member knows, has been one of the laggards among Canadian industries in the recovery movement, and
(3)	to make it possible for home owners throughout Canada to make long-needed repairs and improvements to their homes.
With regard to the experience in connection with a similar plan in the United States, may I say that in that country the plan is known as the modernization credit plan, and was initiated in the summer of 1934 under title one of the Federal Housing Act. It has now been in operation for over two years, and has met with striking success. In the first twenty-two months of operation, namely up to June 1 of last year, a total of 1,056,000 individual loans had been made in the United States for an aggregate amount of $382,000,000. In an official booklet issued by the federal housing administration of the
United States under date of July 20, 1936, the following statement is made:
Losses of the 6,289 financial institutions which have made loans under the modernization credit plan and which have been paid by the federal housing administration have to date totalled less than one-half of one per cent of the total amount of their advances. A survey made in the early part of 1936 showed that these loans on the whole had had an excellent record for prompt repayment. At that time only a fraction over two per cent of the total number of loans were in default thirty days or more. A total of 4,333 financial institutions reported that they had no accounts that were delinquent thirty days or more.
That is the experience of the United States plan up to June of last year, as officially reported.
Later information indicates that by the end of 1936 close to $500,000,000 had been borrowed under the plan in the United States, and the authorities there estimate that for every dollar borrowed, private capital has spent an additional $3. On that basis they have arrived at the conclusion that a $2,000,000,000 construction repair program has apparently been the result. No up-to-date figures as to actual losses in the United States are available, but it is estimated by the authorities of that country that they are still less than two per cent, and that the actual eventual loss to the government will be under one per cent.
In the original United States plan the government of that country guaranteed the lending institutions against loss up to twenty per cent of the total amount of loans. Later the insurance against loss was reduced in that country to ten per cent, and provision was made for increasing the limit of loans up to $50,000 with respect to certain larger properties such as apartment houses, manufacturing and industrial plants, colleges, churches, hospitals, business and commercial buildings, and so on. In this legislation we are not contemplating going beyond the home.
In connection with the amount of the guarantee, I would say that while we have provided in the legislation and in the resolution now before the committee for a guarantee up to fifteen per cent of the amount of the loan, judging from the experience in the United States I believe that the losses incurred will be only a fraction of that amount. However, it appeared essential that if we were to achieve the success we had in mind we should remove any hesitation which might otherwise be evident in the attitude of the lending institutions. Consequently, a fifteen per cent guarantee is asked for. I think the attitude of the lending institutions is at least in part the result of this decision, especially
Home Improvement Loans

in view of the fact that in the United States the lending institutions secure a much higher rate on the government guarantee home improvement scheme than we are proposing to allow under the legislation of which this resolution is a necessary preliminary.
This is all I wish to say in the way of a general statement. I think the details with respect to terms and conditions and standards and all the rest of it can be discussed much better when the bill is in the hands of hon. members. The bill will be distributed just as soon as the resolution is concurred in.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with great attention to the explanations given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). Every hon. member of this house is favourable to the improvement of Canadian homes, but it seems that such improvements should be made by those who already have the money to make them. There are thousands and thousands of men throughout the country who have money deposited in the banks, and who are keeping it there instead of spending it on home improvements. Since 1930 many people have been sitting on their money instead of spending it. They have been waiting for the proper time to spend SI,000,
82.000,	85,000 or perhaps S10,000 to build a barn, to purchase land for a son, to paint a house, to build a store, and so on. They are not yet spending their money as freely as they did when this government was previously in power before July, 1930. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) left the people of Canada a wonderful souvenir when he presented that budget which showed a surplus of over 840,000,000. That was a long time ago, and we have passed through some strenuous years.
Before giving an opportunity to people who have no money to get some from the banks, it would be much easier to induce those who have money to spend some of it. The results can be seen from the bank clearings. The last year my hon. friend was minister of finance, before July, 1930, the bank clearings amounted to $20,000,000,000. The year after, under the guidance of the leader of the Conservative party, who was then minister of finance, the bank clearings dropped down to
815.000. 000.000. People got very tight with regard to money matters because they had very little confidence in the government of the day.
Before passing such legislation as is proposed, two things should be done. First, we should fire all the Tories which the previous government put into strategic positions, and, second, we should repeal every piece of legisla-

tion passed by that government. If that were done, public confidence would be restored and people would begin to spend their money more freely. It is all very simple: we do not need any legislation. Fire the Tories and drop the Bennett legislation into the wastepaper basket. Then the people throughout the land will breathe easier.
This is one of the ideas of the employment commission. I do not believe in supermen or wizards. The chairman of this employment commission is a so-called wizard, but we do not need any wizards in this country. What we need is people with common sense.

I was not referring to the hon. gentleman, but if I were it would be in connection with " cents." I was referring to "sense." This idea really came from the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. McLarty), who suggested it to the chairman of the commission. Here is what will actually happen. Joe has poor credit while John has good credit at the banks. They will both go to the bank to try to get $500 to improve their homes. Joe will get nothing because his credit is no good, while John will get the $500 he asks for. But he would get it even if there was no such legislation. If his credit is good he will get the money right away, whereas if his credit is no good, he will get no money from the bank. All this legislation actually changes nothing. We will have to come back to the good old policy of firing all the Tory strategic *men and dropping the Bennett legislation into the wastepaper basket. When that is done business will be good throughout the land.
The second idea brought forward by the employment commission was the classification of the unemployed. This idea was suggested by the member for Temiscouata. He carried on this classification himself, and then it was continued very efficiently by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). This work vras dene without the help of the commission; the ordinary staff in the department were able to do all that was necessary. Since September this work has been in charge of the employment commission, but we have heard nothing of it. It is being done by wizards, which probably means that it will never be seen. Work like this should be done right away and not continued over the centuries. I suggest to the chairman of the employment commission, to spend some time on this idea of the classification of the unemployed. Let

Home Improvement Loans
him work on it instead of making useless speeches on the housing scheme. This is my very humble suggestion about the matter. I may say that I dlo not believe in the enactment of more legislation; there is already too much of it. A very eminent financier, Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, has spoken of the enormous number of laws that we have in this country, laws that nobody is supposed to ignore. Next session it would be better, and I suggest this to the government, if they simply brought down the estimates and the necessary bills to ratify trade agreements. Let us try a session like that, without futile legislation, and the country, I am sure, will be all the better for it.

speechtext: I want to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance one feature of the act that was in operation last year, because it offers a very serious impediment to proper administration of the act. The clause to which I refer, which withholds the benefits of the act from a certain large class of our population, stipulates that the person borrowing the money must be steadily employed. Automatically that rules out, whether intentionally so or not, the shore fisherman on the Atlantic seaboard. I do not know what is being done on the Pacific coast, but on the Atlantic coast and in the maritime provinces the banks are taking advantage of the fact that a man must be steadily employed before he can come under the act. We all know that a fisherman's occupation is seasonal, and the amount he receives in any year depends on what he gets for his catch. The homes of our fishermen are badly in need of rehabilitation. A great many of them are living in buildings that would not be tolerated by any other class of the community except those living in the outports of the dominion. This is one clause of the act which I think calls for revision.

speechtext: I think my hon. friend (Mr. Hartigan) must be speaking of the housing act and not of the proposed legislation with respect to home improvements, which of course as yet has no existence.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
No, I am speaking of the alteration and improvement loans that we had during the past year.
Mr. TOLM1E: Is it the intention of the government to issue loans strictly on the merits of the property in question, or are certain districts to be favoured first? I ask the question because in the neighbourhood

of Victoria when some people have applied for loans they have been informed: We propose, to begin with, to lend only in certain districts, ignoring others. I consider that is hardly fair, and I would like to know what is the intention of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: My hon. friend is confusing this proposed legislation with the present housing act. I have had no such complaint with respect to the two months' operation of the home improvement plan. Under the housing act, as my hon. friend knows, the complaint he is now making was a very general one, especially in British Columbia. But any owner of a home, who is credit worthy and desires to make improvements, can get from a chartered bank or any of a number of other institutions, details of which I will give on the bill, a loan under the terms of this home improvement plan, which is entirely separate and distinct from the housing act.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: I thoroughly understand that. I know quite well the property to which I refer. I sold the land, to begin with, on terms to the man who proposed to build the house, so that I am fairly familiar with the situation. What I was asking was whether it was the intention to favour certain districts or to lend them money on the merits of the property in question. In this case the man is a first class risk; I regarded him as one to whom a sale could be made on credit. He has constructed his house to a certain point, but it is not finished, and he wants to take advantage of this scheme in order to complete the building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
I can hardly understand, under the circumstances referred to by my hon. friend, how a man could be refused a loan under the home improvement plan by any branch of any chartered bank, because that is the basis of the scheme. There may be something in connection with the credit worthiness of the individual concerned about which I know nothing, and about which, perhaps, my hon. friend knows nothing. If loans have been refused for any other reason than that the borrower is not in the view of the lending institution credit worthy, or that the money is not to be used for the purpose contemplated by the scheme, I have not heard of it. These are virtually the only two valid reasons for refusal of loans, and one of the things that have pleased me most is the very small number of complaints of people not being able to make use of the facilities provided for by the plan. I have felt up to now that the banks and other lending institutions concerned have been cooperating whole-heartedly in getting it going

Home Improvement Loans
in a large way. There will be cases, of course, where a prospective borrower will think he ought to get credit when the lending institution thinks he is not likely, for reasons which appear good to them, to be able to repay the loan. We are not compelling the lending institutions to lend where they do not think a loan would be repaid; they must have reasonable confidence of that. I take it, in the case that my hon. friend mentions, he at any rate would be willing to lend the money, because the borrower is a good risk, and if that is so there should be no reason why the borrower cannot demonstrate to a bank that he is a good borrower and, provided he comes within the terms of the scheme as provided by the bill which will be introduced following this resolution, he should be able to get the loan.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: I shall be glad to give the minister further particulars in the form of a letter.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Absolutely; that is what I say. This scheme is devised for the individual on his own credit, without endorsement and without collateral security. That is why the government is standing behind the scheme,-in order to make it easy for people who have character and credit, and can assure the bank of their ability and willingness to repay, to get a loan without note or collateral, in the simplest possible way. That is why the scheme has started off so successfully. In spite of the winter season, SI,200,000 has been lent in small amounts in less than two months. All this, of course, will develop during discussion of the details of the bill itself.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
That is not being
carried out in my constituency. Anyone who applies for a loan must have someone to back his note before he gets the money.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

speechtext: I should like to have the particulars, because one of the conditions is undoubtedly the one I have stated. subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: May I support what has been said by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., (Mr. Tolmie), and also pass on a suggestion to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning)? The bank, taking the attitude they have maintained for the last five years, said that the locality did not warrant a loaur, although the man was definitely of a good type to whom money could be lent, and is well employed. It may be said that the banks are justified in taking this attitude, but I bring the matter to the attention of the minister so that in his instructions to and deliberations with lending institutions he may point out that where a man is financially in a position to borrow, the locality of his residence should not particularly affect his entitlement to a loan.

a little misunderstanding on the part of some of those who have spoken. The government has not undertaken under this plan to direct that banks shall make loans. The banks must make their own decision, based upon the exercise of discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Right.

But if they do make the loan-without endorser, too; they have no right to ask for an endorser or for a second name-the government underwrites it to the extent of fifteen per cent against loss. subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS

If I meet my engagement promptly, then of course it is just a banking transaction between the bank and myself, but if at the end of the given time the bank finds that fifteen per cent of its advance has not been paid, up to that point the government will reimburse. No member of this committee is more anxious to see our working men better housed than I am, but I believe this bill is starting at the wrong end. I am confident that there are sufficient funds awaiting investment in the hands of private individuals to build all the houses necessary in this country, but these funds are not so used because if a man builds a house in any city or town in Canada he cannot sell it for more than fifty per cent of what it cost him. That is where the trouble lies. Years ago a man could buy a lot, build a house and rent it and make some money out of it; to-day the costs of labour and material and taxes are so high that it is impossible for people to make such investments profitably. subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: This discussion is simply leading to confusion as between the housing act and home improvement loans. To my mind this home improvement proposal is the most sensible and practical one which has ever been put into legislation. In the first place it relieves the government of overhead charges; it places the responsibility upon the banks. No hon. member can expect a man to be able to go into a bank and borrow money unless the bank thinks the loan will be repaid. The man must be a home owner to start with. The difference between this proposal and the housing act is that the lending companies who lend money for the construction of a house consider material collateral. In this matter they simply consider a man's moral worth and likelihood of repayment of the loan. And it is not a matter of thousands of dollars but of a few hundred-to improve one's bathroom or kitchen, to add a room, and so on. As for private loans, one hon. member suggests that there is plenty of private money available. Let me tell you, you can have plenty of difficulty in getting a private loan, and the rate of interest will be higher than it will ever be on a loan from a bank, if your moral standing is good.

speechtext:
I should like to know whether the bill will cover a case like this: I have in mind a very worthy and thrifty working man who came here from the old country-he is perhaps only one of many in the same class-who bought a piece of land, paid for it, and commenced to build a little home. In the first place I believe he built two rooms. He saved a little money and added two more rooms. In the building of the house the roof necessarily had to be flat, because it was only one storey. Now he desires to add another storey and have a hip roof, and to modernize his plumbing a little. He has no debt of any kind; his property is clear. What would that man, who at the moment requires something less than $750 on a

property worth $3,000 or $3,500 have to do to borrow the $750? Could he go to a bank or lending institution, get the money and proceed with the work without engaging a solicitor or someone to intercede for him when the loan is being negotiated? If the bill covers such a situation as this I can see that it will be of tremendous benefit to hundreds, perhaps thousands, of working men of the class I have mentioned, and will result in considerable increase in employment in the building trades and allied industries, such as lumber, hardware, plumbing supplies, and so forth.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIR OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: It is very difficult to give an answer with respect to a specific case, especially in view of the fact that my hon. friend approaches the matter from the wrong angle. Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for,
(a)	the surrender by the Minister of Finance of certain amounts of the capital stock of the Canadian National and the Canadian Northern railway companies,
(b)	the transfer and exchange of certain shares of the capital stock of the said companies,
(c)	the abandonment of certain claims against the Canadian National Railway Company,
(d)	the adjustment of certain accounts affecting government railways,
(e)	the setting up of a securities trust corporation for the purpose of preserving the priority rights of the dominion and its protection against future contingencies in respect to potential interest and other savings, and
(f)	generally for revision of the accounting set-up of the Canadian National railway system.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is customary to discuss a resolution of this kind before the house goes into committee. In view of the fact that it involves many intricate matters with respect to money and finance, without in any sense committing ourselves to the principle of the resolution I am prepared to agree that the Speaker leave the chair and the house go into committee, on the understanding that by so doing we are in no sense acquiescing in what under some circumstances might become a very dangerous piece of legislation, depending upon what the legislation may be as outlined by the minister.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the resolution indicates, the bill to be founded on the resolution involves important changes in the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways. In the first instance it will provide for the centralization of capital stock control of the companies now comprising the national railway system, through one company, namely, the Canadian National Railway Company. At the present time the Canadian National Railway Company includes the Grand Trunk railway and about sixty subsidiary companies. On the other hand the Canadian Northern Railway Company includes the old Canadian Northern railway with about forty subsidiary companies. These two companies are entirely separate corporations, both owned by the Dominion of Canada, the only connection between them being a common board of directors.
C.N.R.-Accounting

The financing for both the Canadian National and the Canadian Northern is carried out through the Canadian National Railway Company, so that through the funding of maturing obligations and advances for capital purposes the debt of the Canadian Northern is gradually being transferred to the Canadian National, even though the Canadian National Railways have no direct stock control of the Canadian Northern Railway.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Does it not own all the
stock?

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: No.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: The Canadian National Railway?

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
No, the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway is owned by the Minister of Finance, or the federal government. Similarly the government railways are in a rather anomalous position. Under the act of 1919 the government railways were entrusted to the Canadian National Railways for management, with the proviso that the account of profits or deficits would be for the consolidated fund. In the financing act of 1923 and in subsequent financing acts this arrangement has been modified, so to-day the deficit account or profit account of the Intercolonial and other government railways is included in the consolidated balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways. But the control by the Canadian National Railways is far from definite, and this whole situation requires some clarification. The bill will provide also for the bringing of the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways into conformity with the net debt of Canada. At the present time there is a duplication between the net debt of Canada and the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways which has reached the staggering sum of 81,-
500,000,000 and which is pyramiding annually.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: It is not pyramiding as a national debt; it is pyramiding only on the books of the railway.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
But it is pyramiding as a duplication. I have noted this frequently in financial journals and I had it brought to my attention quite forcibly a short time ago during a discussion with a prominent man who was investigating the finances of Canada. The debts of the railway are a liability of the government as long as the railway does not earn sufficient to cover them, and the usual practice by analysts interested in dominion finance is to add the net debt of Canada to the debt of the Canadian National Railways as shown

in the balance sheet. If that is done the obligations of Canada are shown to be about $5,750,000,000, which is entirely incorrect. This figure is arrived at because of the duplication to which I referred. The real position is that the responsibilities of Canada with regard to debt on account of both dominion and railway obligations amount to about $4,250,000,000. I think this is a very important matter and one which should be corrected. If this pyramiding of duplicated debt is allowed to continue it is bound to affect the credit of Canada very materially, as well as the credit of the Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: It is only the interest that is being pyramided.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: In 1932 the pyramiding of deficits was put an end to, but the pyramiding of interest goes on. When I tell you that to-day the interest alone, which is included as funded debt of the railway, amounts to $495,000,000, you will appreciate that it is pyramiding in an extraordinary way.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Has money been borrowed
to meet these interest obligations?

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: This interest has never been paid and has never been shown on the government books as due. Under the legislation governing the accounts of the Canadian National Railways it must be shown as a debt of the railway in the balance sheet. To that extent it duplicates the national debt.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Have there not been
occasions when the government was obliged to borrow in order to meet the indebtedness of the railway?

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: This has no relation to the obligations of the railway to private investors.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: I was referring to interest charges alone.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Fifty-five per cent, was
it not?

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext:
Sixty per cent, I think. I
believe the government owned forty per cent, which it had obtained in compensation for guarantees and one thing and another.
As I was saying, the board of arbitration found that sixty per cent of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway was worth $10,800,000, which would make the total stock of the railway worth about $18,000,000. It is proposed to surrender $82,000,000 of this stock which has no value, and to write into the balance sheet the remaining $18,000,000 of stock which was found to have full value. This $18,000,000 will be exchanged for new stock of Canadian National Railways, which will represent common stock ownership of the railway, and which of course will be wholly owned by the dominion government.
That is a brief outline, Mr. Chairman, of the changes in the balance sheet. Of course, when the bill is brought down, the details will be shown, with very complete explanations in the bill. In any event the bill will be sent to the committee on railways and shipping, where it will be studied very fully.

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: The minister might deal with paragraph (e).

subtopic: REVISION OF ACCOUNTING SET-UP
speechtext: That deals with the securities trust corporation. I may say, Mr. Chairman, that the revision of the capital structure has been before the house on many occasions, and has always been the subject of debate when the Canadian National Railway estimates have been before the house. The reports of the committee on railways and shipping also indicate that similar discussions take place there every year. The government has always taken the view that no change in capitalization could properly be
Accounting
made as long as any feature of the Canadian National accounts was in dispute; that is, as long as lawsuits were pending, the capital position of the railway should not be changed.
What is the present position of that lawsuit? Is it through?

The Lovibond case, yes. I
have a statement here but I think I can give the gist of it. The privy council ruled that Lovibond has no claim against the government of Canada. They also ruled that he has no case against the Canadian National Railways for having the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway restored to the books. The privy council did give him permission to sue the railway for damages, and they said in their judgment, "for what it is worth," indicating that they thought his claim was not very serious. However, in order to preserve all the priorities in the case it is proposed that the claims of the government which are being eliminated as funded debt from the balance sheet shall be preserved in a securities trust, a company within the corporate structure of the railway and the stock of which will in turn be wholly owned by the dominion government. These claims of the government that are eliminated from the balance sheet will be maintained in this securities company, where they can be used at any time to maintain the priority of the government equity as it now exists. In that way I think we can say that the priority of any outstanding security or any outstanding claim against the railway will not in any way be disturbed by the change in the capital structure now proposed.
This change in the capital structure involves no change whatever in the net debt of Canada. Any claim against the railway on behalf of the government which is regarded as an active asset is maintained in exactly the same position. The change in capital does not involve the writing out of the balance sheet of any amount that was expended on the railway for capital purposes, that is, which created an earning asset of the railway, although its position is being changed from bond interest to proprietors' equity.
In regard to the Intercolonial and other government railways which were entrusted to the Canadian National Railways, these railways are included in the balance sheet as proprietors' equity. These railways were paid for by the dominion government as they were built, and their present position in the balance sheet as a funded debt against the railway is hardly proper under the circumstances.

That is a general review, Mr. Chairman, of the subject matter of the bill. The details will be printed in the bill itself, and the bill is printed with very complete explanations of the changes proposed.

With respect to the indebtedness to consolidated revenue of about $600,000,000, and accrued interest of $500,000,000 odd, is that interest of $500,000,000 being carried to the trust account? Does it still remain a liability of the railway? What becomes of it? Was any portion of it ever guaranteed by the government?

The interest referred to,
$495,000,000, is the interest due to the dominion government itself for funds it advanced to the railway.

Out of consolidated
revenue fund.

Yes. This interest is being written out of the balance sheet of the railway. It is a duplication of the consolidated fund, because no asset in the consolidated fund is set up to correspond with it. This $495,000,000 of interest will disappear from the balance sheet of the railways but will be carried in the securities trust for the purpose of preserving whatever priority the government has in connection with these claims against the railway for interest.
'Mr. POULIOT: Mr. Chairman, I hold in my hand Hansard of April 27, 1936, in which there is a speech by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) at page 2200, where he says this:
The minister has referred to the president of the Canadian National system. I have a high regard for him.
I am not speaking; it is the right hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Bennett) who is speaking through me. He went on:
He was in Calgary, working with the Canadian Pacific Railway, when he was taken by Mackenzie and Mann as master mechanic, and he has risen to a position of importance, but it is my duty to say this, that, temperamentally he cannot resist pressure. He cannot, in that sense, say no. The pressure of politicians, members of this house, members of the government, is such that he cannot resist it; that is the pressure, not of the opposition, hut of the powers that be. I say that with the best intentions in the world, and I say so because I know whereof I speak.
Afterwards our venerable colleague who sits for one of the constituencies of Montreal, St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. White), protested very strongly against the language used by his leader in connection with the president of the Canadian National Railways.

C.N.R.-Accounting
The questions I ask the leader of the Conservative party, the right hon. member for Calgary West, are these: When did he notice first that Mr. Himgerford was weak and could not resist pressure? Was it before he himself appointed Mr. Hungerford president of the Canadian National Railways, or was it afterwards? If it was before, was it on account of the fact that he found Hungerford was weak that he appointed him, to please the Canadian Pacific Railway? If it was afterwards, why did he not cancel through his own government Hungerford's appointment as president of the Canadian National Railways? I have written a series of articles in a weekly which is published at Riviere du Loup, and which the right hon. gentleman probably reads because he quoted from it during the last session. The questions I have put to him are most serious. Here is the most important job in the business of our country, a job equal to that of president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, one that needs a strong man. The so-called strong man who was at the head of the government of that time chose a weak man, and, having chosen him, he says, "I know whereof I speak." I will ask the right hon. gentleman to be kind enough to answer the three questions I have just put to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The debt is about $700,000,000, translated into our money?

If you put it that way, yes, about $700,000,000. The road is a narrow gauge one, three feet six inches wide. Last year they operated the road on a ratio of 58 per cent of its takings, without depreciation, and after allowing for depreciation it cost only 65 per cent of its earnings to operate the property. The important part of this interesting document is the detail with which the investment of the people of South Africa in the property is indicated.
So far as I am concerned I was pleased to hear the minister say to-day that he thought it undesirable that there should be any change in the capital structure as long as that litigation was pending in respect of the shares. When we came into office in 1930 we found this threat of litigation, and it continued until after Mr. Lovibond finally got the case to the privy council. Particulars of his statement of claim were placed upon Hansard in answer to a vigorous complaint made by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Euler, that we had failed to deal with the reduction and readjustment of the capital stock as suggested by the auditor and by the then chairman of the trustees. I pointed out the reasons why we had not done so, and I think they were wholly adequate ones, because if the judgment which Mr. Lovibond had hoped to get had been obtained the question as to the shares in the Grand Trunk being properly vested in the Minister of Finance would have been at issue. As the matter now stands, the statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) represents my appreciation of the situation, namely, that Mr. Lovibond may maintain an action for damages, with what success the future may disclose, but that would be an action which would be founded purely in damages and would be disposed of by a monetary payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will not affect title at all.

No; as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) says, it will not affect title. That is an entirely different question from the one that obtained when the judgment of the privy council was given.
I may say frankly to the committee that it was a matter of some relief to me to see that judgment, because there have been grave differences of opinion as to whether this parliament could adequately vest in the Canadian Minister of Finance shares of a company whose head office was at Dashwood House, in London. But I always felt that the answer was to be found, not as a pure matter of law, in just a legal proposition, but rather in the conduct of the parties, and that it was not

C.N.R.-Accounting

competent for the railway company, in view of what had taken place, to make any such contention as that. The ground of the decision, however, was technical; it does not touch that phase of the matter at all; and we may now eliminate from our consideration any question which arises with respect to the shares themselves and realize that any action which may possibly be maintained will be an action founded in damages and not against the shares themselves.
There are three matters that must engage the attention of anyone concerned with a readjustment of the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. The first is the properties which belong to the crown, and which we speak of as government railways. They comprise the Intercolonial railway so-called and all the other properties which have been acquired which were branch line feeders of that property; they also comprise the line from Winnipeg to near Moncton, namely, the National Transcontinental and various other connections with that line. The Prince Edward Island line I classify as part of the Intercolonial. We have here a definite investment which is reflected in part in the national debt of the country and in part by payments made out of surplus revenues during days of buoyant and large revenues in this dominion.
The method by which that expenditure can be dealt with in a set-up or balance sheet is not one which for the moment I am going to discuss. The minister says that he proposes to send the bill to the committee, and the committee doubtless will have the opinion of the auditors who made the suggestion as to the set-up, and will arrive at a conclusion as to the best way to deal with it. There are many methods of dealing with it, but the cold fact is that in any report made to the people of Canada it is in my judgment essential that they should know that since confederation the people have invested so many millions of dollars in the Intercolonial, the Prince Edward Island railway, the National Transcontinental railway, and the branch lines and various undertakings subsidiary to and connected with that large government railway enterprise.
The minister referred to this investment being dealt with as owner's equity. I do not think that term conveys anything to the people of Canada in dealing with this matter. It need not be an item in the balance sheet itself in the narrow sense of the term, but in the wide sense a report of the Canadian National Railways should never be issued

which does not make apparent to any person who reads it the amount of the investment by the Canadian people in what we call government railways.
That is, preserved in the balance sheet.

Yes, that is all it is necessary they should know. I am not very particular as to how it should appear, but I am concerned that the Canadian elector who reads that balance sheet shall be able to know, for his own interest and his own welfare, just how much money has been invested in the railways and their appurtenances since confederation. That is number one.
Number two is the investment made by the Canadian people in the Canadian National railway system. It will be recalled that the Canadian National system was reorganized by the Borden administration with a capital of $100,000,000. That this was done against my protest, and that I voted against it-
Excuse me; I think the amount is $165,000,000. They exchanged the Grand Trunk-

No; I am speaking of the Canadian Northern. The second branch is the Canadian Northern system. It will be remembered that the Borden government reorganized that system by creating out of the various constituent and subsidiary companies a new organization known as the Canadian Northern system, capitalized at $100,000,000. That I personally thought that capitalization greatly excessive or that I voted against my own friends on that occasion is not a matter of interest now. But I did protest as strongly as I could against the property not being allowed to go into the hands of a receiver. We set up a new system, known as the Canadian Northern system, with a capital of $100,000,000. That system transferred to the Canadian people a certain percentage of its capital stock, I think some 40 per cent, or $40,000,000. As compensation for that the Canadian people advanced to the system $45,000,000, partly paid, as the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) mentioned the other day, by the issue of promissory notes of the Dominion of Canada in the shape of $1,000 bills.
Then the war came. But the result of the first transaction on the part of the Borden government was to create a new transportation system known as the Canadian Northern system, which comprised railways in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Nova Scotia and one small line in Quebec.

C JVJt.-Accounting
It is worthy of note at this point that practically every province except Prince Edward Island, and I think Quebec, was concerned with the Canadian Northern system as a guarantor of its securities. That is a matter of tremendous importance in dealing with the set-up of the balance sheet. The province of British Columbia guaranteed the securities of the Canadian Northern (British Columbia), and from- the proceeds of the securities thus guaranteed Mackenzie and Mann built that line from the great divide between Alberta and British Columbia down into the city of Vancouver. They also built certain lines in the Okanagan district, and undertook certain contractual obligations with respect to hotels and other matters. Bear in mind, however, that that undischarged guarantee of the province of British Columbia was the basis of the construction of the British Columbia section of the Canadian Northern railway system, and that from day to day and from year to year since the consolidation, British Columbia has not been called upon to pay that guarantee but the Canadian taxpayer has himself absorbed it and is from day to day making the payments which otherwise would have had to be made by the' province. If that is kept in mind, the extent to which the Canadian, taxpayer has prevented the bankruptcy of that province will be realized, because it wouldi have been financially impossible for British Columbia during the years of the great depression to pay the guaranteed interest upon those securities.
In Alberta a number of guarantees of the same kind were outstanding. On the strength of the legislation and the guarantees the bonds and securities were sold by Mackenzie and Mann and the money deposited in a trust account, and there is yet a part of a right of way from Calgary to Macleod as a memorial to the optimism of the people and the capacity of great contractors to induce the people to take action which was wholly unnecessary. The road has never been built, but part of the money was expended and the remainder was in a trust account when last I investigated.
In Saskatchewan guarantees were given more largely to the Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines company than to the Canadian Northern system. There again, as in the case of British Columbia and Alberta, the people of Canada are discharging the obligations arising under those guarantees, which, if added to the already impossible burden that these provinces are carrying, would have made it quite beyond the realm of possibility for
them to stagger on. That obligation of those three provinces has been discharged by the Canadian people since the consolidation of the system into the Canadian National.
Then we come to Manitoba. In Manitoba a very difficult situation exists. There are the old Canadian Northern lines of Mackenzie and Mann; the old Northern Pacific lines, to which, as hon. members know, the province succeeded, and the province making its arrangement with the Canadian Northern. There are, in addition, guarantees given with respect to terminals, branch lines and main lines, and there is certain legislation enacted by this parliament to deal with that situation. The consequence is that the province of Manitoba is committed to guarantees on a scale which it is quite impossible for it to meet-I think that is a fair way to put it-which guarantees the Canadian people are now paying instead of the people of Manitoba.
In Ontario just before the election of 1911 guarantees were given by this parliament on the Canadian Northern Ontario railway, the section in that province. And certain land grants were made available for the system under conditions to which I need not now refer. There was, I believe, one small line, a very small one, guaranteed in the province of Quebec. In New Brunswick the National Transcontinental ran to Moncton and thence went off on the Intercolonial to Halifax or Saint John. I think the guarantees, as far as the people of New Brunswick are concerned, were given to lines which since have been merged in the Canadian National system, rather than to the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk. New Brunswick was saved from bankruptcy by reason of our assumption of the obligations created by the guarantee given by the government of the day on the Halifax and South Western road, which was constructed by Mackenzie and Mann from Halifax around the coast. In Prince Edward Island there was nothing to get, so that no railways were guaranteed there.
That is the picture in regard to number two. How are you going to set it up in your balance sheet? In 1917, it will be recalled, the government of the day was pressed to acquire the balance of the Canadian Northern shares, and the question as to whether this should be done by arbitration or through the exchequer court was considered by the parliament of that day, sitting in the Victoria museum.	Finally it was
decided to have it done by arbitration. Three arbitrators, the chief justice of Nova Scotia, the chief justice of Ontario and the late Wallace Nesbitt, constituted the arbitration tribunal, and they decided that the remaining
C.N.R.-Accounting

60 per cent of the shares was worth $10,800,000. But I believe it was clearly demonstrated by the evidence which was given that the shares were worth nothing, and but for what took place in this chamber I do not think the arbitrators ever could have awarded anything, because instead of the shares having value, they certainly were a liability. But they were given a value of $10,800,000, which was $800,000 more than the maximum which the statute provided should be paid for the shares. Allowing that 60 per cent is worth $10,800,000, it follows that 100 per cent is worth $18,000,000, and in my judgment the minister is dealing generously with the situation when, on the balance sheet, he carries those shares at $18,000,000. That is what he proposes to do. In my judgment they are worth considerably less than that, but the matter is one which need not be discussed now. It is ancient history; I expressed my views on that subject some twenty years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The shares never were
worth it.

Of course not. I come
now to the third factor in the balance sheet which is dealt with by this resolution, namely the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and allied organizations. This is neither the time nor the place to deal with the situation as it arose in connection with the Grand Trunk. Personally I would have let it go into the hands of a receiver, but again my views were only those of one man, and very unimportant at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was one other.

We determined to deal with these railways in another way; certain securities were settled with on the basis of an annuity, to put it shortly, and the value of the other securities was to be determined by arbitration. That arbitration by a majority decision decided that the shares had no value. Against that judgment, of course, the old Grand Trunk people have ever since protested, and at times they have made it rather difficult for us in London and elsewhere because of the contentions they have made. During the few weeks or months we were in office in 1925-26, I came to the conclusion that the sound thing to do was to bring to the knowledge of the British people the real facts in connection with the Grand Trunk; for if one wants to read of high finance developed to its nth degree in connection with the payment of dividends and the disbursement of money, one has only to read the evidence given at the arbitration in connection with those matters.

The subsidiary companies, the Grand Trunk Pacific, Grand Trunk Pacific Townsites, and so forth, perhaps need not be referred to here beyond saying that what we paid for the Grand Trunk system and its subsidiary companies is represented by an annuity, and nothing else. And when I say an annuity I mean the interest upon the senior securities which we took over practically at par and which we need not now discuss because they were not the subject matter of either arbitration or expropriation. Their value was fixed by agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Pacific did go through receivership.

I was coming to that. The Grand Trunk Pacific, while it was a subsidiary enterprise of the Grand Trunk system, was a separate entity. I am sure all good Liberals who read the history of it must do so with a sense of pride. I cannot resist saying that, though I am endeavouring to be most moderate in my criticism. At any rate the Grand Trunk Pacific did go through a statutory receivership. The Minister of Railways became the receiver, and ultimately the late Sir Henry Thornton made an adjustment with respect to the securities, which are now part of the obligations of the Canadian National system with which we have to deal from time to time. I might have said the same with respect to certain income securities issued by the Canadian Northern.
That is the third factor we have to deal with in the balance sheet. I think the minister is wholly justified in writing out absolutely the Grand Trunk common shares and the other shares, because we paid nothing for them, and if my logic is sound there should not appear in the balance sheet a successive valuation upon anything in that balance sheet. Therefore, as far as the Grand Trunk and its subsidiaries are concerned, we can write out the value of those common shares.
Those are the three factors. To-day they constitute what we speak of as the Canadian National railway system, but there are no Canadian National railway shares in the sense in which we usually speak of a corporate enterprise. To all intents and purposes the Canadian National is a holding enterprise. In reality the Minister of Finance holds the shares; I am considering the Minister of Finance as being the same thing as the Canadian National.
The Minister of Finance is the holding company.

Quite so, but the operations are carried on by the Canadian National. Perhaps as a matter of exactitude I should

C.N.R.-Accounting
say that the shares are vested in the Minister of Finance, unless the procedure has been changed. I take it that they are still so held.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are still held by the Minister of Finance.
Yes.

That was not always the view expressed, mark you. I am happy to hear the minister take that view, because some of the officers of the road on one occasion went so far as to suggest to me that it would be desirable to write the enterprise down to what it was worth. How is one going to determine what it is worth? What we want to know is what we put into it, and the amount on which we have to pay interest.
The second question asked by the hon. member is this:
2. What is the total annual interest on this indebtedness?
And the answer is: $49,184,622.87 in 1936. That is the sum of money which, if our railway system were successful, it would be earning, in addition to any other sums, to enable it to square-and I use a word which is sometimes used-or to clear itself with regard to its accounts.
Had it been successful it would not owe any such sum, because a large part of that is deficit, and interest on deficits.

Yes, but that is a separate matter, and I shall come to it later on. Remember, Mr. Chairman, that I have endeavoured to put before the minister this- and so far he has agreed with me-that we have an indebtedness of $1,184,612,248.59 of the Canadian taxpayers' money tied up in our railways. For the year 1936 to the end of December it cost the Canadian people $49,184,622.87 to service that debt. It cost that much to pay interest on the sum invested. My submission is that it must always be clear to the Canadian people what sum they have had to pay by taxation and otherwise from year to year to discharge the interest on the obligations incurred for the railways. I am talking about the public only-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is very difficult.
I do not like to interrupt my right hon. friend at this point, but-
It is quite all right.

-we may as well discuss these points as they arise. May I point out to the right hon. gentleman that in its legislation of 1932 the late government really stopped

the historical record, that is, as to the funding of deficits. I do not see how the historical record suggested by my right hon. friend can be maintained, even if no change is made. We might give the deficits of past years, but we stopped giving them in 1932, so that the whole picture is really not a correct statement. That is, the balance sheet of the railway does not show the total funds advanced by the government to the railway for capital and deficit purposes, with interest compounded annually.

I am afraid the minister has not been following the matter prior to coming to the house. In 1932, when the Duff commission was appointed, it dealt with the matter and made a recommendation stating that it was undesirable to issue the company's securities for deficits guaranteed by the government, but that the government should borrow the money itself and pay the deficits.
Yes.

Therefore, so far as the securities items on the railway company's accounts are concerned, the balance sheet does not show. But they should show that to pay those deficits they got the money from the Canadian people.
But the balance sheet does not.

That is what I contend they should have done. I have asked them to do it, but it was not done. I had no control over it, because the trustees were in complete control. I do not think their views were in any greater harmony with mine than with those of the Minister of Transport.
I say without question the sums of money the Canadian people had to borrow to pay for the deficits on that road from year to year should be apparent in the accounts of the system, so that the Canadian people, the shareholders, may know what they had to borrow to keep their property afloat. That is the position I have always held, and I submit that anything less could not be regarded as satisfactory. If we do otherwise we are not being fair with the Canadian people.
My position with the officers of that system is a simple one. I simply say to them, "I want a balance sheet that shows to me as a citizen and a shareholder how much money the Canadian taxpayer had to put up last year to keep this property afloat. That is all I want." Anything less than that I cannot but think is a form of deception-not practised deliberately, possibly-upon the

Canadian people. In other words if they assume, from looking at the accounts, that because there is nothing showing, and because it is not indicated that they had to borrow so much money to pay their obligations during the year, all is well, they are living in a false paradise.
