I am not going to discuss the matter in further detail, much as I might be disposed to do so, because when the minister said he proposed to send the bill to a committee it appeared to me that it is for men more expert than I am in matters of this kind to explain and to suggest what would be a proper system of accounting. I think the committee will agree with me when I say that whatever set-up may be finally agreed upon, it

CJV.-ffi.-Accounting
should be a statement which will show to anyone who studies it just what have been the expenditures by the Canadian people in our railways. That is number one.
The next point is that, although it 'may not be part of what one might call the consolidated balance sheet, it could easily be shown as part of the annual statement so that there would be no difficulty in understanding on the part of any one. I think the minister is anxious, and I know every hon. member is anxious, that with respect to our railroads we should know just what we have done. I do not believe any hon. member is satisfied by being told that we had a deficit of S40,000,000 or $50,000,000 last year; what he is anxious to know is how much it has cost Canada to run these railways.
If I were disposed to give a chronological history of the railroads of this country I am sure it would be very difficult for any one within sound of my voice who belongs to the Liberal party to explain how two transcontinental lines came into being. I have never met such a man in later years although I used to meet him occasionally in earlier years. I can remember during the progress of a debate in the old chamber when one member suggested that I favoured three systems. The late Mr. Oliver had made some observations about having built up two systems and my cynical interruption was, "Three systems." It was then stated later on that I favoured three systems.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, oh.
I do not wonder that the hon. gentleman laughs. In my own community I was condemned as a pessimist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was said about me too.

Whoever said that was not very familiar with my public appearances. I advocated to the extent of my ability that there should be a second system. I happened to be in Edmonton when the Canadian Northern was opened for traffic to that city on September 1, 1905. I wonder if many members in this chamber realize what limitations were placed upon the guarantee which Mr. Blair gave Mackenzie and Mann. Do they realize that Mr. Blair provided that there should be no amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific? When I lived long enough to see this effort made to put three transcontinental systems across the Dominion of Canada, I but ventured to prophesy what came to happen. I do not think I was ve.y much of a prophet because I was successful in my anticipations. I could not see how anyone could have done otherwise.
But I am not concerned about the past. Recriminations serve no useful purpose with respect to these matters. There is one thing I do feel very strongly, that is that the balance sheet as finally made up should be such as will enable every Canadian to know without difficulty just how much money successive governments have compelled the taxpayers of this country to pay. That is not unfair, is it? That is not asking too much, is it? Anything I have to say will be predicated entirely upon that assumption. I did not think we could reach this matter to-day and I did not bring with me the report of the government railways in South Africa. This is a volume of many pages and it deals with every phase of their railway life. I think it will make us feel that there is still room for more improvement.
Cannot we get this matter out of politics? During the last election I was charged everywhere in the country with being an enemy of the Canadian National system. I dare say that not more than five per cent of Canadian National employees who were electors voted for the candidates of my party, that is outside those employees who voted for purely personal reasons for candidates in a particular locality. I dare say that dollar for dollar I am as much interested in the success of the Canadian National Railways as most people. Every failure of the Canadian National to meet its obligations means more taxes for the Canadian people. Let there be no misunderstanding about that. If it does not meet its annual expenditures the minister has to borrow money with which to pay them, or he must get it out of surplus, which means taxation of the Canadian people. No citizen of this country, however poor he may be, has not a direct interest in the success of this system. It touches his economic life as no other single thing in the state does. There are combinations of many things which may concern him more, but there is not a single thing which concerns him so closely.
Do hon. members realize what the raising of the interest on the public debt and providing for these deficits mean? As I mentioned last session, it means the providing of so many dollars per minute or even per second. Every citizen is concerned. We are often anxious to make matters appear better than they are, and I ask the minister to keep in mind what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said the other day about conferences. His statement should be applied to these balance sheets. Let these balance sheets reflect the facts; let them indicate the full extent of our liability and our financial responsibility, so that eveiy Canadian
C.N.R.-Accounting

will be interested in giving his support and assistance toward the successful operation of his property. It is his property, not somebody else's. It belongs to us, not to somebody else. In my judgment the only way in which a sense of responsibility can be developed is to show the people the financial side of this question, what it means in taxation, what it means in interest on the national debt and in the payment of deficits. All this has to be borrowed from the public and they must be made to realize that the success of the railway means a lessening of the burden of taxation. To the extent that taxation is lessened, the personal prosperity of the people is increased.
When I rose I had not intended to speak at such length on this matter, as the minister said that he was going to send the bill to the committee on railways and shipping. It seems to me that that method will provide an opportunity for everyone concerned to express his opinion and for those who are expert in the adjustment of figures on balance sheets to make such suggestions as in their wisdom are necessary. I hope the minister will keep this one thought in mind, that the balance sheets should reflect the true financial condition of the enterprise so that every citizen of Canada may know without difficulty the exact extent to which he and those who went before him have either placed out real money or borrowed money for the purpose of making the enterprise part of the assets of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I have been sitting here quite impatiently for the last fifty minutes and I cannot say that I have listened very carefully to what the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) has said. What he took fifty minutes to say he could have said in ten had he cut out all repetition. You are presiding, sir, over a committee made up of seventy-nine members of this house. May I ask each one of the other seventy-eight members of the committee if the hon. member for Calgary West has answered my .questions. They were fair, very easy to understand, and spoken in very plain language. I want an answer, Mr. Chairman. The right hon. member for Calgary West stated, according to page 2200 of Hansard of April 27, 1936, that he had realized that Mr. Hungerford was weak. Now he is the gentleman who appointed Mr. Hungerford as president of the Canadian National Railways, a most important job. I ask him now, When did he realize that Mr. Hungerford was weak, according to his own statement? I ask him if it was before Mr. Hungerford's appointment by the right hon. gentleman himself or if it was

after, and if it was after, why did he not discharge Mr. Hungerford on account of that weakness? This is no joke, sir. The right hon. member for Calgary West said, "I know whereof I speak." It was probably not the first time he said it, but he said it on that occasion. I should like to have an answer to those three questions, if you please.
Oh, no answer? I shall sit down then because I should like to have an answer; it is very important. No answer? There will be a long speech, a long lecture on everything, and I am surprised the right hon. member for Calgary West has not given us the name of the first locomotive between Montreal and Laprairie. He was telling the story of the railways, and he could have told us that, as well as the length of the locomotive, the number of wheels, and all that. That is the kind of story we listen to in the house when we have important business to carry on. Now I ask him a question concerning a position of the greatest importance, equal to that of the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am not a rich man, but I am a good Canadian citizen, just as good as anybody else, and I should like to know why the right hon. gentleman appointed Mr. Hungerford as president of the Canadian National Railways if he thought he was a weak man, and I shall ask him, further, if it was not because he thought he was a weak man that he appointed him to that position.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Howe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 12, to provide for revision of the accounting set-up of the Canadian National railway system.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Dairying, $290,000.
May I ask the minister the reason for the increase of 118,000 in this item, and what is the purpose of the vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
The item of $290,000 which the
committee is being asked to vote this year is made up of proposed expenditure on administration, $13,500, which is $1,900 more than was spent last year, but the largest item in the vote is for the dairy produce division, $226,000, an increase of $7,500 over

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
last year. The estimate for the dairy markets division is 841,000, an increase of $6,300 over last year; the estimate for the dairy research division, $5,000, an increase of $800 over last year; the estimate for milk utilization service, $4,500, an increase of $1,500 over last year.
The increase of $1,900 for the administrative division comprises $1,400 for printing and stationery and $500 for travelling expenses. In the dairy produce division, there is an increase of $9,775, for travelling expenses, but against that there is a decrease in other branches of the service, so that the net increase is $7,500. In the dairy markets division there is a total increase of $6,300. There is an increase of $156.60 for communication services. In order to take care of the purchase of a thermograph and repairs to same, the amount for equipment has been increased by $500. Under miscellaneous current expenses there is an increase of $12.50, and other increases as follows: salaries, $2,166; general supplies, $225; refrigeration car service, $1,500; travelling expenses, $1,740- and that increase is largely to take care of the travelling expenses of the new supervisor of condensers-dairy research division, increase of $800-and this is made up of an increase of $181 for supplies for dairy research laboratory-an increase of $25 in transportation charges for materials, and it has been found necessary to increase the amount for travelling expenses by $594. In the milk utilization service the increase is $1,500. This includes an increase of $25 for communication services. There is also an increase of $25 in the amount for wages for assistants at exhibitions. The amount provided for travelling expenses for 1936-37 was found to be less than required, and it has been necessary to increase this amount by $1,450. This makes a total increase of $18,000.
What does the minister propose to do in connection with dairy marketing? In what way is he going to expend the increased grant which has been made for that purpose?

I just gave the explanation, in reading from the items that are contained in this appropriation: dairy markets division, an increase of $6,300. It has been found necessary to increase the amount for communication services by $156.60. That is a very small item of increase in the matter of communication expenses. In order to take care of the purchase of thermographs and repairs to the same, the amount for equipment has been increased by $500. That increase does not necessarily mean that there is any particularly increased service; it is a
matter of buying thermographs and paying for repairs to them. Under miscellaneous current expenses an increase of $12.50 is shown. In salaries an increase of $2,160 is made necessary on account of the appointment of a supervisor of condenseries. It is not an additional service. It shows an addition in this particular branch, but it has been taken out of another branch, and the individual who was doing this work before in one of the other branches is now appointed in this one, with this particular title. The other amounts are small.

I asked the question because, although we hear a great deal about improved conditions, we have not improved conditions in the dairy business. As regards our butter and our cheese we are very slightly better off than we were a year ago, and the d,airy farmer is not receiving any participation in what is called the return of prosperity-It is true that we in Canada have been manufacturing the best cheese in the world. It commands in the British market a higher price than any other make except the English cheddar, and it has lately been displacing that, because they are not making it in such large quantities as formerly. The cheese we are producing and exporting is selling in the British market to-day at a premium of two cents per pound over the best New Zealand cheese. That speaks for itself. We cannot say so much for our butter. We cannot compete with New Zealand as regards butter, and if we were to export our butter to-day we should have to take at least five or six cents per pound less than we are getting on the local market. To-day our local markets are no better than they were a year ago. By that I mean that the dairymen are not participating to any very great extent in the return to prosperity.
In respect of the increase in salaries, I should like to know whether it represents increases in the salaries of the present staff or an addition to the personnel of the staff.

So far as the references to the condition of the dairy farmer are concerned, I think the figures indicate that those statements are scarcely in accordance with the facts.
As regards the price of cheese, the average increase last year, taking the year through, over the previous year is 2-6 cents per pound. That is a very considerable increase when one remembers that a year ago cheese was selling at around ten to eleven cents per pound. The average increase over the year of 2-6 cents is a very considerable percentage of the price we were obtaining at that t'me.

The Late Hon. Charles Marcil
May I ask the minister where he obtained those figures?

I obtained them from the records of the department, and I believe an examination of the records generally will indicate that to be true. It is just six o'clock, and probably it would be well to discuss this matter at greater length after we return at eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Progress reported.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, since the house rose at six o'clock we have had word of the death of Hon. Charles Marcil, one of our members, the oldest in point of service in the house, and a former Speaker. On discussing the matter with such members as I have been able to reach in the meantime it was felt that it would be a fitting tribute to his memory if this house adjourned. I therefore move that the house do now adjourn.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I desire to associate myself with what has been said by the Minister of Finance. I think it is entirely fitting and proper that this chamber, out of deference and respect and regard and esteem for its oldest member in point of service, and one who has been the first commoner of Canada, should now adjourn.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 8.0S p.m.
